main_message: Steel power has always been about controlling the path from raw materials to market. Carnegie did it by owning everything, governments now do it with tariffs, quotas and a golden share, and Europe is adding a carbon toll that changes which steel is cheapest.
why_hook: The 88 million vs 82 million tonnes contrast and 'guarded like a weapon' make a clear puzzle. But the numbers come fast, and the 4% share only makes sense after a second of thought.
what_connects_layers: The 'who controls the path, who sets the toll' idea ties them together. Carnegie owned the path, governments restrict access to it, and carbon pricing taxes it. It's neat, but it feels a bit imposed on the history. The jump from Carnegie to the EU carbon rules is big, and the hydrogen section is a loose end.
ending_comment: It answers: steel power is about share and control of the path, not tonnage. It then admits it can't say whether the cost is worth it, which is honest but a little unsatisfying. The Braddock closing image is nice.

boring_or_slow.why: Lots of tons and miles of ore, coal and limestone. Easy to lose the thread.
Coke fields, stock purchases and acreage figures are dense and dry, apart from the Homestead moment.
A string of proclamation dates and percentages (Feb, Jun, Apr, Jun) blurs together.
A pile of OECD numbers, one after another.

confusing.quote: seventy-one percent electric... eleven in China
confusing.why: I'm told to 'hold on to' these numbers but don't know why until segment 10. Also unclear why scrap-based furnaces matter.

confusing.quote: capacity utilization rose from seventy-two to seventy-seven percent
confusing.why: I don't know what capacity utilization means or why 80% is the target.
The explanation is long and legalistic, and the 'consent rights' detail is hard to follow.
CBAM jargon. The 190 vs 57 euro math is hard to follow without a visual.
Vague. I don't know what 'machine' means until segment 12.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: Chinese steel exports hit a record
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: It leans on the OECD's overcapacity and subsidy story, with no Chinese side and no mention that China's growth fed the world's building.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: power over the people who worked it, at a cost no price list shows
felt_biased_or_one_sided.direction: sympathetic to workers, critical of Carnegie
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: It's a mild editorial aside, but one-sided.

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: hurt the competitiveness and employment of American manufacturers
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Evidence about 2002 tariffs is set against the administration's own claims, which slightly tilts toward tariffs not working.

claims_you_doubt.quote: whoever controls the cheapest path... sets the price
claims_you_doubt.why: A big claim from one 19th-century example, presented as a general rule.
Plausible, but stated without much support.

claims_you_doubt.quote: steel power was never only about tonnage
claims_you_doubt.why: A neat conclusion, but the video never shows that share or path control actually protects anyone, so it feels asserted.

claims_you_doubt.quote: a toll changes which paths are cheapest
claims_you_doubt.why: I'm not shown that CBAM has actually shifted any steel trade yet.

best_moment: 09: Biden blocks the deal, Trump allows it, then the golden share is used to force a plant reversal. It's concrete and surprising, and it ties old Pittsburgh to today. Runner-up is the Homestead battle in 04.
top3_fixes: Explain jargon in plain words when it first appears (capacity utilization, golden share, CBAM certificates, electric arc furnace vs blast furnace), and say why the 71% vs 11% numbers matter right where they're introduced.
Cut the number density in 03, 04, 07 and 08: keep one or two striking figures per segment and move the rest to on-screen visuals. Replace the proclamation date list with one simple timeline.

Define the 'machine' and 'path vs toll' idea early, in segment 1, and make the hydrogen section either show its link to the thesis or shorten it. Add a balancing line on the Chinese perspective and on whether the tariffs worked.
